item.text: {"question_id":"1B.1","answer":"In 2023, China under Xi publicly advanced several risk-reducing proposals, including crisis prevention, no-first-use discussions, lower alert levels, safeguards against unauthorized launch, nuclear-facility safety, nonproliferation, and dialogue on emerging-technology risks (BATCH-0016-E002; BATCH-0017-E002; BATCH-0023-E001). Xi also personally stated that China opposed nuclear war, supported talks over Ukraine, and would not exploit the crisis for gain (BATCH-0018-E008). These records establish declared positions and one diplomatic initiative, but not completed implementation, resourcing, or measurable risk reduction. Against them, open-source evidence shows substantial force and resource expansion: China’s arsenal increased in size, accuracy, readiness, and diversity; new silo fields and dual-use delivery systems expanded possible theater-strike and coercive options; and 2023 military spending rose 6 percent, with much of the increase directed toward PLA combat readiness (BATCH-0005-E006; BATCH-0007-E017; BATCH-0023-E012; BATCH-0025-E028; BATCH-0025-E029; BATCH-0025-E030). These developments increased strategic uncertainty and could reduce warning time, although the evidence does not prove a first-use decision, launch-on-warning adoption, or a prestige or personal-power motive. Xi held formal authority over changes to China’s nuclear forces, and one cited scholar described his personal planning of strategic-force construction, but the precise 2023 directives, approvals, objectives, and causal responsibility for individual changes remain uncertain (BATCH-0025-E031). Overall, the evidence supports mixed declared restraint alongside risk-increasing modernization and readiness choices, with implementation and intent
